meta.titre: Population Structure and Ageing: dependency ratios, pyramids and demographic change
meta.sous_theme: Age structure, dependency and population ageing

sections.contenu_markdown: A secondary school in Yaounde or Bamenda holds hundreds of young people, while many villages in the same country have a growing number of elderly residents. Governments must plan schools, jobs, hospitals and pensions for these different age groups, and the balance between them is measured by the dependency ratio. Papers 1 and 3 ask you to calculate it from a table, Paper 3 also asks why the true figure may differ and what immigration does to it, and Paper 2 asks you to argue whether the world has a problem of too many people or too few. This course covers all three.

items: The birth rate is the number of live births per 1,000 people in a year, and the death rate is the number of deaths per 1,000 people in a year.
Life expectancy is the average number of years a person born in a given year is expected to live.
Migration is the movement of people between places; immigrants move in and emigrants move out.

sections.titre: Age structure, the dependency ratio and the effects of ageing
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Population structure
Population structure is the composition of a population by age and sex, shown on a pyramid. Three groups matter: **youth** (children and teenagers), **adults** or working-age population, and the **aged**. The common bands are 0 to 14, 15 to 64 and 65 and over, but some questions give their own bands. Always use the bands in the question.

### The dependency ratio
$$\text{DR}=\frac{\text{youth}+\text{aged}}{\text{adults}}\times 100$$
The youth dependency ratio uses only the youth, and the old-age dependency ratio uses only the aged, both divided by the adults and multiplied by 100. A ratio of 80 means 80 dependants for every 100 adults. The ratio is only an estimate of the true economic burden. Adults who are students, unemployed, disabled or unpaid carers do not earn, which raises the real burden above the ratio, while children who work and elderly people who still farm reduce it.

### Pyramid shapes
An **expanding** pyramid has a wide base and steep sides (high birth rate, many young dependants), as in many African countries with youthful populations. A **stationary** pyramid has nearly vertical sides (low birth and death rates). A **contracting** pyramid has a narrow base and a wide top, as in Japan and several European countries.

### Causes and effects of ageing
Population ageing comes from falling fertility and rising life expectancy. Effects include higher costs for pensions and health care, a shrinking workforce, a smaller tax base and shortages of workers. Responses include later retirement, pro-birth policies, training and automation, and welcoming working-age immigrants.

### Immigration
Immigrants are mostly young adults, so they swell the working-age group and can lower the dependency ratio in the short term. They may later age and bring dependants, so the effect can fade.

### The global debate
World population is still rising, but the growth rate has slowed because fertility is falling in most regions. Some countries now shrink and age, while growth stays rapid in parts of sub-Saharan Africa. Hence the problem differs by region.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a table gives the numbers in each age group and asks for the ratio or for the country with the highest ratio.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Write the formula, substitute the numbers from the table, give the answer as a number per 100 adults and round sensibly. When asked which country has the highest ratio, calculate every country; do not judge from the size of one group.

variantes.nom: How far do you agree questions
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to assess a statement about world population with a number of arguments.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give each argument for the statement and each argument against it with evidence by region, then a judgement that says the problem varies: some regions face ageing and decline, others still face rapid growth. A strong answer qualifies the statement rather than accepting or rejecting it entirely.

sections.enonce_markdown: The age structure of a fictitious country Z, in millions, is: youth 18, adults 30, aged 6. (a) Calculate the dependency ratio, the youth dependency ratio and the old-age dependency ratio. (b) Explain why the real burden might be higher than the ratio suggests, using the fact that 6 million of the adults are unemployed or in full-time study. (c) Calculate the new dependency ratio if 2 million working-age immigrants arrive.

etapes.action: Write the formula and extract the data.
etapes.justification: The ratio compares dependants with the working-age group.
Use the same denominator, the adults, for each ratio.

etapes.action: Explain why the actual burden is higher.
etapes.justification: Not every adult produces income, so the true number of workers is smaller than the adult group.
etapes.resultat_markdown: If 6 million of the 30 million adults are unemployed or in study, there are only 24 million workers. Dependants become $18+6+6=30$ million, so the burden is $\dfrac{30}{24}\times100=125$ per 100 workers.

etapes.justification: Immigrants of working age enlarge the denominator and leave the other groups unchanged.
A comparison shows the effect of each change.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Immigration lowers the ratio from 80 to 75, while counting unemployed and student adults raises the effective burden to 125.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The dependency ratio is **80**, with a youth ratio of **60** and an old-age ratio of **20**. The real burden is higher, about **125 per 100 workers**, once non-working adults are counted. If 2 million working-age immigrants arrive the ratio falls to **75**.

items.erreur_markdown: Dividing the dependants by the total population: $\dfrac{18+6}{54}\times100$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The dependency ratio compares dependants with the working-age group, not with everybody. Using the total understates the ratio.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving the answer as 0.8 or as "80 people" without saying "per 100 adults".
items.pourquoi_faux: The dependency ratio is conventionally expressed per 100 working-age persons. A bare decimal or a number of people is not what the formula gives.
items.correction_markdown: Multiply by 100 and state the meaning: "80 dependants for every 100 adults".

items.erreur_markdown: Using the bands 0 to 14, 15 to 64 and 65 and over when the question defines youth, adults and aged by other age limits.
items.pourquoi_faux: The question's table is built on its own bands. Substituting different bands uses numbers that are not in the table.
items.correction_markdown: Use the figures for the groups exactly as the question labels them.

items.erreur_markdown: Reading a pyramid with a narrow base as a sign of a high birth rate.
items.pourquoi_faux: A narrow base means that few children are being born. A wide base signals a high birth rate.
items.correction_markdown: A wide base shows high fertility and a youthful population; a narrow base with a wide top shows low fertility and an ageing population.

items.erreur_markdown: Claiming that ageing is only a problem of rich countries and rapid growth is only a problem of poor ones.
items.pourquoi_faux: Both situations exist across the world: some developing countries are also ageing and some regions still grow rapidly. Such an answer is too general.
items.correction_markdown: State that the balance varies by region and support each side with a named type of country or region.

items.enonce_markdown: A country has 12 million youth, 24 million adults and 4 million aged. Calculate (a) the dependency ratio, (b) the youth dependency ratio and (c) the old-age dependency ratio, correct to one decimal place.

The table gives the populations of three fictitious countries in millions.

| Country | Youth | Adults | Aged |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 9 | 21 | 5 |
| Q | 14 | 20 | 3 |
| R | 6 | 25 | 9 |

(a) Calculate the dependency ratio of each country and state which is highest. (b) Say which country has mainly youth dependency and which has mainly old-age dependency, with figures.
items.solution_markdown: (a) P: $\dfrac{9+5}{21}\times100\approx66.7$. Q: $\dfrac{14+3}{20}\times100=85.0$. R: $\dfrac{6+9}{25}\times100=60.0$. **Country Q has the highest ratio, 85.0.** (b) Q is dominated by youth dependency: youth ratio $\dfrac{14}{20}\times100=70$ against an old-age ratio of 15. R is dominated by old-age dependency: old-age ratio $\dfrac{9}{25}\times100=36$ against a youth ratio of 24.

items.enonce_markdown: Country S has, in millions, youth 15, adults 30 and aged 6. Twenty years later the figures are youth 12, adults 32 and aged 12. (a) Calculate the dependency ratio at each date. (b) Describe how the composition of dependency has changed. (c) Suggest two measures the government could take, and say one drawback of each.
items.solution_markdown: (a) First date: $\dfrac{15+6}{30}\times100=$ **70**. Second date: $\dfrac{12+12}{32}\times100=$ **75**. (b) The ratio has risen even though youth have fallen: youth dependency fell from 50 to 37.5 while old-age dependency rose from 20 to 37.5, so dependency has shifted from the young to the old and the pressure moves from schools to pensions and health care. (c) Raise the retirement age (drawback: older workers may be less able to continue and young people may find fewer vacancies); encourage working-age immigration (drawback: social tensions and a later rise in the aged group); introduce pro-birth incentives (drawback: costly and slow to take effect). **Any two measures with a drawback each carry the marks.**

items_markdown: Dependency ratio equals (youth plus aged) divided by adults, multiplied by 100; use the age bands the question gives.
The youth and old-age ratios use the same denominator, the adults; the total is their sum.
The real burden can be higher than the ratio when adults are unemployed, studying, disabled or caring; working children and elderly lower it.
A wide-based pyramid shows high fertility; a narrow base with a broad top shows low fertility and ageing.
Immigration of working-age adults lowers the ratio at first; the effect fades as migrants age and bring dependants.
The global problem varies: ageing and decline in some countries, rapid growth in others, so answers need regional evidence.
